summary: Skyblink is a free, public web tool that lets anyone hunt for moving and changing objects in NASA's SPHEREx all-sky survey. You type a star's name, a Gaia catalogue ID or sky coordinates, and Skyblink finds every SPHEREx image of that spot in NASA's IRSA archive and plays them like a little movie, the same way Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930 by flipping between two photographs. Anything that moves or changes stands out. Images can be subtracted to make motion jump out, combined into sharper stacks, and narrowed to a single infrared wavelength. Clicking a star measures it in every exposure, giving an infrared spectrum on the fly, its brightness over time, a search for repeating patterns, and a forecast of its next visit. It answers the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge directly: it works on all five test targets, shows Barnard's Star moving and RW Aurigae fading by about half in a year, and picks up new SPHEREx data releases automatically. It runs in any browser, including on a phone, with nothing to install, so students, amateur astronomers and citizen scientists can help search a sky that no one can check alone.
details:
What it does. Skyblink turns SPHEREx's spectral images into a blink comparator anyone can use. A visitor enters a position (a name, a Gaia DR3 ID, or RA and Dec) and a radius of up to 7.5 arcminutes. Skyblink shows every SPHEREx image of that patch as a flip-book, one frame per visit or one per exposure, in any of the six detector bands or at one chosen wavelength. Gaia stars are circled where their motion puts them on each date, pixels flagged by the SPHEREx pipeline can be highlighted, and every view is saved in its URL so it can be shared or embedded.

How it works. A Python (FastAPI) server searches NASA's IRSA archive for every SPHEREx image covering the position, then reads only the needed bytes of each image straight from NASA's public cloud copy, instead of downloading a 65 MB file per exposure. It subtracts the mission's zodiacal-light model, turns each patch north-up, and streams the patches to the browser as they finish. The browser does the rest: it stacks each visit's exposures on a grid three times finer than SPHEREx's 6-arcsecond pixels, blinks and subtracts them, and measures the marked star in every exposure. Because each SPHEREx exposure sees a slightly different wavelength, those measurements form a spectrum from 0.75 to 5 micrometres. A period search (Lomb-Scargle) removes each visit's colour trend and checks candidates against the telescope's own observing schedule. Google's TimesFM model forecasts the star's spectrum at the next visit, and reports how it did on a held-out visit.

Results. All five test targets load (258 to 1,764 exposures each). Barnard's Star's motion is obvious in a single subtraction. RW Aurigae faded from about 2,300 to about 1,200 mJy at 4.27 micrometres within a year. All 358 exposures of Barnard's Star load in about 47 seconds.

Limits we know about. WISE 0855 is too faint to see in the images. Six-arcsecond pixels hide slow movers. With only three visits per star so far, period candidates are leads to check, not discoveries. The forecast was tested on one star (21% average error, against 33% for repeating the previous visit).

Why it matters and what is new. Volunteers blinking images have already found most known comets and brown dwarfs. WiseView does this for the older WISE survey; Skyblink brings it to SPHEREx and adds what only SPHEREx makes possible: a spectrum from every click, sharper stacks from many shifted exposures, and a search for brightness changes. It needs no install and no account.

Tools. Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy and fsspec on the server; JavaScript and HTML canvas in the browser; three.js for the presentation; Google TimesFM 3.0 for forecasting; hosted on Vercel, with the forecasting model on a separate home server.

Use of SI tools. Parts of the code and text were written with help from an AI coding assistant (Anthropic's Claude). The forecast uses Google's TimesFM, a pretrained foundation model. All images shown are real telescope data; none are SI-generated.
